passage: Last month Rehana had told the class that Delhi was in the south. Half the room laughed, and the teacher had to bang the desk. Since then her hands stayed under the desk during every lesson. Today the teacher asked about the rivers of the north. Rehana knew the answer, because she had read it three times, but her lips only moved. Raghav, who had laughed loudest that day, shouted a guess and was wrong. This time nobody laughed. He looked around, and Rehana saw him swallow. The teacher waited, looking gently in her direction, then moved on to the next question. Rehana's hands stayed under the desk.

qa.q: What had Rehana said about Delhi last month?
qa.a: Rehana had told the class that Delhi was in the south.

qa.q: Why did Rehana keep her hands under the desk even though she knew the answer?
qa.a: Rehana seems to fear being laughed at again, so she protects herself by staying quiet, even though her lips moved with the answer.

qa.q: What could the teacher try to help Rehana speak again?
qa.a: The teacher could speak to Rehana privately, ask for answers in small groups first, and keep stopping mockery quickly so that it feels safe to be wrong.

qa.q: What might Raghav be feeling when he swallows after his wrong guess?
qa.a: Raghav may feel a flicker of the embarrassment Rehana felt, now that he is the one who was wrong in front of everyone.

grounding: A child who was laughed at for a wrong answer stops volunteering, protecting herself by staying quiet while her potential goes unseen.

passage: Marek's turn to read aloud came in three desks. He counted ahead and saw that his paragraph was the one with “muscle” in it. Last term he had said it wrongly and the whole circle had snorted. Now he bent over his desk and searched his bag for a pencil that was already in his hand. Layla, who sat next to him, saw his hands shaking. The teacher said, “Marek?” and Marek shook his head. “Not today,” the teacher said, and moved on. Layla read his paragraph in a rush. At break Marek sat at the far end of the bench, alone, still murmuring the words under his breath.

qa.q: Which word did Marek worry about in his paragraph?
qa.a: Marek worried about the word “muscle.”

qa.q: Why did Marek search his bag for a pencil that was already in his hand?
qa.a: Marek seems afraid the class will laugh again like last term, so he pretends to be busy to avoid reading; his shaking hands show how nervous he is.

qa.q: What could the teacher try so that Marek reads aloud again?
qa.a: The teacher could let Marek practise the paragraph privately first, and keep any teasing from happening so that reading feels safe.

qa.q: What might Layla have been thinking when Layla saw Marek's hands shaking?
qa.a: Layla may have felt sorry for Marek and wanted to help, which fits reading his paragraph in a rush to take the pressure away.

grounding: A child who was laughed at for a wrong pronunciation stops volunteering and protects himself by staying quiet.

passage: Note from the Class 6 science teacher, Thursday. Payal used to be the first hand up. Since the quiz on 12 August, when she said the moon makes its own light and Baljeet and a few others laughed loudly, she has not volunteered once. Today I asked her directly about plant roots. She knew it; I saw it in her notebook later. But she said, 'I don't know,' and looked down at her desk. Baljeet glanced at his friends. After class I spoke to Payal alone and told her that her notebook answer was right, and that laughing at answers is not allowed in my room. Tomorrow I will set a class rule about this with everyone, and speak to Baljeet privately first.

qa.q: What did Payal say about the moon at the quiz?
qa.a: That the moon makes its own light.

qa.q: Why did Payal say 'I don't know' when she knew the answer?
qa.a: She was afraid of being laughed at again and felt safer staying quiet than risking embarrassment.

qa.q: What is the teacher planning to do, and why does it help?
qa.a: Set a class rule against laughing at answers and talk to Baljeet privately first, so the class becomes safe again without shaming anyone.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be thinking when he glances at his friends?
qa.a: He may be checking whether they'll laugh again, enjoying the attention, without seeing how much his laughing silenced Payal.

grounding: A teacher's note on a child who stopped volunteering after being laughed at, hiding what she knows to stay safe.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Maths today. Miss asked who could solve the sum on the board. I knew it. I really did. But last week, when I said seven eights are fifty-four, Sonu and his gang laughed so loudly that even the class next door heard. Sonu kept saying 'fifty-four' at lunch all week. So today I kept my hand under the desk. Farida got it right and everyone clapped. I had the same answer in my rough book. I checked after.
Mummy asked why I'm so quiet these days. I said I'm tired. It's easier to be invisible than to be the joke.
Maybe next week.
Irawati

qa.q: What answer did Irawati give last week for seven eights?
qa.a: Fifty-four.

qa.q: Why did Irawati keep a hand under the desk today?
qa.a: Irawati felt scared and embarrassed about being laughed at again, like last week, so staying quiet felt safer.

qa.q: What small step could help Irawati feel safe to answer again?
qa.a: Telling Mummy or Miss about the laughing, so the teacher can stop the mocking in class.

qa.q: How does Mummy likely see Irawati's quietness?
qa.a: Mummy notices it and is concerned, but only hears 'tired', so she doesn't yet know about the laughing.

grounding: A child laughed at for a wrong answer stops volunteering and hides a right answer to avoid being mocked again.

passage: In the government school at Kallur, the English teacher asked Ramesh to read the next line aloud. He read 'Wednesday' as 'Wed-nes-day', the way it looked. The back row burst out laughing, and Harish repeated it in a squeaky voice all through lunch. The next week, when the teacher asked who could read, Ramesh stared hard out of the window at the goats grazing in the field. At home he read his whole English book to his little sister by the lantern, every word, quick and clear. But in class, whenever a question came, he shook his head. The teacher wrote 'shy' in the register and moved on.

qa.q: How did Ramesh read 'Wednesday'?
qa.a: As 'Wed-nes-day', the way it looked.

qa.q: What does Ramesh reading well at home but shaking his head in class suggest?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and afraid of being laughed at again, so he hides his ability in class.

qa.q: What could the teacher do instead of writing 'shy' in the register?
qa.a: Stop the mocking, speak to Ramesh privately, and give him a safe chance to read, perhaps to the teacher alone first.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's little sister see him?
qa.a: She hears him read quick and clear every night, so she likely sees him as a good reader, unlike his classmates.

grounding: A village boy mocked for a mispronunciation stops speaking in class, and his real reading ability goes unseen.

passage: In Mrs Dlamini's Grade 5 class in Durban, Thabo used to answer everything. Then, in October, she asked where rain comes from, and Thabo said, "From the sea, when it gets tired." Rafael snorted first, then half the room joined in. At lunch someone said "tired sea" in a squeaky voice, and it followed him for weeks. Since then Thabo keeps his hand flat on the desk. Last week Mrs Dlamini asked why ice floats. Thabo whispered the answer to himself, exactly right, and stared at his pencil. Rafael answered wrong, and nobody laughed at him. When reports came home, Thabo's said "quiet, participates little". His grandmother read it twice and frowned. "You?" she said. "Quiet?"

qa.q: What did Thabo say when asked where rain comes from?
qa.a: He said, "From the sea, when it gets tired."

qa.q: Why did Thabo stay silent even though he knew why ice floats?
qa.a: He was afraid of being laughed at again; the sting of the "tired sea" joke made staying quiet feel safer than being right.

qa.q: How could Mrs Dlamini support Thabo now?
qa.a: She could stop mocking as soon as it starts, talk with Thabo privately, and give him low-risk ways to share, like writing an answer before saying it.

qa.q: How does Thabo's grandmother see the report?
qa.a: She is puzzled, because the Thabo she knows at home is not quiet; the report describes a child she doesn't recognise.

grounding: Shows a child who was laughed at for a wrong answer stop volunteering, so his real ability goes unseen at school.
